options.text: No — it is only Base64url-encoded and readable by anyone; the signature only proves integrity
Yes — the payload is fully encrypted and secret
Yes — only the server can read any part of it
No — but the payload cannot be read without the private key

questions.explanation: A signed JWT's payload is just Base64url-encoded and readable by anyone; the signature makes it tamper-evident (if verified), not confidential — so never put secrets in it.

questions.prompt: Match each session-cookie attribute to what it protects against.

pairs.right: The cookie traveling over plaintext HTTP
The cookie being sent on cross-site requests (CSRF)

questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts, Secure keeps it off HTTP, and SameSite blocks cross-site sending — together hardening the session ID.

questions.prompt: What must a server always do with a JWT it receives? Select all that apply.

options.text: Trust the claims without checking, since it looks valid

questions.explanation: The server must verify the signature, check expiry (and issuer/audience), and pin the algorithm; trusting an unverified token lets an attacker forge claims.

questions.prompt: To defeat session fixation, the server should ____ the session ID at login.
questions.explanation: Regenerating the session ID at login ensures an attacker-set ID from before login can't be reused to ride the authenticated session.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to set up a secure server-side session.

items.text: Create a session with a long random ID
Issue the ID in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie

questions.explanation: A secure session uses a random ID, a hardened cookie, ID regeneration on login, and destruction on logout — giving real revocation.

questions.prompt: Which standard should you use to authenticate a user ('sign in with...')?

options.text: OpenID Connect (an identity layer over OAuth 2.0)
Raw OAuth 2.0 access tokens as proof of identity
A plain session cookie with no server record

questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization, not identity; OpenID Connect adds an ID token to actually authenticate the user, so use OIDC for login.
